title: Let's be honest with students about exams and learning
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Prompted by a friend's thirteen-year-old daughter sitting twelve exams in a week and by teenagers on a train calling it all pointless, Skelton tries to answer honestly what exams are for. He argues that exams mainly serve institutions, sifting and grading students for gateways, and that places and cut-offs often matter more than ability. They are summative, rarely help students learn better, and ignore individual circumstances, so they are less reliable than presented. He observes that exam results fade quickly in importance once a student moves on, and that their correlation with later success weakens. Exams are also losing status as AI erodes the middle-range jobs they once unlocked. His conclusion is that schools should stop telling an out-of-date story about exams, since students and families see through it.
points: Exams are largely a device for the organisation to sift and place students, and results are often adjusted through norm-referencing, cut-offs or grade inflation.
Exam systems are mostly summative and do little to improve learning; taking exams is a skill that needs structured repeated practice.
One-off exam sessions can ignore individual needs and so be less reliable than they appear.
Exam pressure is high now but falls to almost nothing later in life, when people are judged on work and on qualities never examined.
The status of exams is falling as the jobs they promised shrink under AI, so schools must stop repeating a dishonest, out-of-date story.
quotes: Mostly, exams aren’t really about students. They are a device to sift and grade them in different ways.
Another way we make choices is by tweaking the system. In the US, there is a currently a debate about grade inflation.

Mostly, exams - in the sense in which we are looking at them - don’t do any of this. They are summative at best; they are an end of learning judgement about what is sticky and what isn’t but with little requirement on them to make learning better.

It is important to learn how to be able to take exams but that learning is a skill that requires repeated experiences. Unless teachers create repeated experiences for their students that help them move through Beginning, Developing and Mastering at levels of how to take a particular exam, it is unlikely that much learning - getting better at taking exams - will be going on.

Quite why a school would ask a pubescent girl who suffers from hay fever to take 12 exams during a hot week in May is beyond me. Quite why they might think this is giving them reliable information on which to base serious decisions about her is beyond me even more.

That’s why so many people who seemed to be successful at school find university hard. It’s why people who are unsuccessful at school are able to successfully take advanced courses later in their lives.
What we can’t do is continue to perpetuate an out of date story about exams, their status and their consequences. Partly because it is dishonest.
